blocks.text: Choosing Your Site Framework

content.value: You're about to

on Barkpark Cloud — a live frontend that reads straight from your content. This guide exists so you can make that choice with open eyes: what each framework is genuinely good at, where it will bite you, and which one fits the site you actually want to ship. There is no single right answer — only the right answer *for your project*.
For most content sites — blogs, docs, marketing, portfolios —
is the best default, and it's the one you can spawn today. If you need a heavily interactive app, you'll want a server-rendered framework like Next.js or TanStack Start. Read on for why.

blocks.text: First, the decision that matters most

content.value: Before the framework, understand the axis every framework sits on. It decides your site's speed, cost, and how much can go wrong.

rows.value: Every page is built once into plain HTML/CSS/JS
Pages are assembled by a live server on each request
Fastest possible — files served from the edge
Fast, but every request does work
Costs grow with traffic; needs a running process
Content that changes on a human schedule
Content that's personalised or changes per-request
The server, under load or on bad input

content.value: Barkpark keeps your

children.value: site and your content on the same wire

content.value: — the site fetches from your Barkpark project over an internal connection, not the public internet. That means faster builds, private reads, and instant updates when your content changes. Static sites get this at build time; server-rendered sites get it on every request.

blocks.text: Why "close" matters here

items.value: — when you publish in Barkpark, your site knows immediately (no manual redeploy).

children.value: No rate limits, no egress fees

items.value: — your site reads content over a private link, not a metered public API.

children.value: One login, one domain, one dashboard

items.value: — the site inherits your workspace, project, and dataset scoping.
— updates roll out with zero downtime, the same way the rest of your Barkpark runs.

blocks.text: The frameworks at a glance

content.value: is a proxy for page weight and speed. Less shipped JavaScript means faster loads and better search rankings — which is why content-first frameworks win on SEO.

blocks.text: The frameworks in depth
Astro — the content-site flagship

content.value: Astro is built for exactly what a CMS produces: pages of content. It renders to static HTML by default and only ships JavaScript for the interactive "islands" you explicitly ask for. If you're building a blog, documentation site, marketing site, or portfolio, this is the one to reach for.
blogs, docs, marketing sites, portfolios, landing pages, changelogs.

items.value: — ships near-zero JavaScript, so pages load instantly and score top marks on Core Web Vitals.
— its content layer is designed to pull from an external source like Barkpark, so the integration is natural, not bolted on.

children.value: Excellent SEO out of the box

items.value: — fast, static, semantic HTML is what search engines reward.
— drop in React, Svelte, Vue, or Solid components as islands; you're not locked into one.
— if you know HTML and a little JS, you can be productive in an afternoon.
— static output means your site is basically free to serve and scales without limit.
— start static, add server-rendering later for the few pages that need it.
of themes and integrations to start from.
— if your site is mostly dashboards, live filtering, or complex client state, Astro's island model fights you.
— sharing state between separate interactive components is deliberately awkward.
than the React/Next world.
than Next's — battle-tested less at very large scale.

content.value: If you're unsure, start here — you can always graduate to a heavier framework later.

blocks.text: Next.js — the do-everything heavyweight

content.value: Next.js is the most popular React framework and can build essentially any kind of site — from a static blog to a full SaaS app. That power comes with weight and complexity.
apps with logged-in users, dashboards, e-commerce, anything that mixes content with heavy interactivity.

items.value: — static pages, server-rendering, and incremental updates all in one framework.
— the most tutorials, templates, integrations, and hireable developers of any framework here.
— if your site has accounts, carts, or dashboards, Next is at home.
— pages can rebuild in the background as content changes, blending static speed with fresh data.
— access to the entire React component universe.
— ships a lot of JavaScript, so pages are slower than a static Astro or Hugo site unless carefully tuned.
— React Server Components and the App Router have a real learning curve, and the "right way" keeps evolving.
— major versions can mean real migration work.
— dynamic pages need a live process, which grows with traffic.
— you'll carry complexity you never use.

blocks.text: TanStack Start — the modern, type-safe challenger

content.value: TanStack Start is a newer full-stack React framework built around the excellent TanStack Router. It prioritises end-to-end type safety and a fast, modern developer experience.
highly interactive, data-heavy applications where type safety and routing power matter.

items.value: — from your routes to your data, mistakes get caught before they ship.
— TanStack Router handles complex, nested, data-driven navigation elegantly.
— built on Vite, so builds and hot-reload are quick.
— streaming server-rendering keeps data-heavy pages snappy.
— smaller community, fewer templates, fewer answers when you hit a wall.
— overkill for a blog or marketing site.
— same running-process cost as Next.
— a smaller talent pool than React/Next.
— APIs are still settling compared to mature frameworks.

blocks.text: SvelteKit — small, fast, and pleasant

content.value: SvelteKit compiles your components away at build time, so the browser downloads very little framework code. It handles both static and server-rendered sites and is widely loved for its developer experience.
teams who want small, fast sites and enjoy a clean, minimal syntax — content or app.

items.value: — the framework compiles itself out, so pages are light and fast.
— concise syntax, less boilerplate than React.
— does static and server-rendering equally well.
— routing, data loading, and forms come in the box.
than React — fewer ready-made components and integrations.
to hire than React developers.
when you choose SSR.
than Next at very large scale.

blocks.text: Nuxt — the Vue powerhouse

content.value: Nuxt is to Vue what Next is to React: a mature, full-featured framework for building both content sites and applications. If your team knows Vue, this is the natural home.
Vue teams building content-rich sites or full applications.

items.value: — years of production use, batteries included.
— a dedicated content module makes CMS-driven sites straightforward.
— flexible per page.
— Vue is often considered gentler to learn than React.
than React-based options.
identical to Next when you go SSR.
than an islands or compiled framework like Astro or Svelte.
— you can't borrow the React component universe.

blocks.text: Hugo — the fastest static builder there is

content.value: Hugo is a single Go binary that turns content into a static site faster than anything else on this list. No Node.js, no runtime — just files. It's a superb fit for large content sites where build speed matters.
large blogs, documentation, and content sites where raw build speed and simplicity win.

items.value: — thousands of pages in seconds.
— a single binary, nothing to keep alive, nothing to patch.
— pure static output, no server code to attack.
— hundreds of ready-made designs.
— mature, with few breaking changes.
— no built-in "islands" story; dynamic bits need hand-rolled JavaScript.
than modern component syntax.
— static only, by design.
than the JavaScript frameworks.

blocks.text: Eleventy (11ty) — dead-simple static

content.value: Eleventy is a minimalist static site generator. It does very little on purpose, which makes it fast, predictable, and easy to reason about.
simple content sites where you want maximum control and minimum magic.

items.value: — little to learn, little to go wrong.
— pages are as light as they get.
and a tiny footprint.
— write pages in whichever templating style you like.
— you add all dynamic behaviour yourself.
— the minimalism means more wiring for anything non-trivial.
than Astro or Next.
— no server-rendering path.

blocks.text: Barkpark Native — the instant, zero-effort site

content.value: Not every site needs a framework. Barkpark can render your content as a live site directly — no build step, no code, no framework to learn. Publish content, get a site. It's the fastest way from "I have content" to "it's online."
getting content live in seconds, previews, and anyone who doesn't want to touch a framework at all.

items.value: — live in seconds, with nothing to build or deploy.
— Barkpark handles the rendering and the updates.
— the site *is* your content; there's no separate copy to fall out of date.

children.value: No runtime to pay for or secure

items.value: — it runs on infrastructure you already have.
— you theme within what Barkpark offers, rather than designing freely.
— if you need pixel-level custom layouts, reach for a framework.
— it's a content site, not an app platform.

content.value: The zero-friction way to get online while you decide whether you need a full framework.

blocks.text: How to choose — by what you're building

rows.value: Content-first, fast, great SEO, minimal fuss
Fast static builds, easy navigation, huge page counts
Fast, SEO-strong, easy to make beautiful
Looks great, ships fast, little to maintain
Mature ecosystem, handles carts, checkout, and scale
Unbeatable build speed at thousands of pages

blocks.text: How your site goes live — and stays live

content.value: Every site you spawn deploys the same way, whether it's Astro, Hugo, or Barkpark Native. The process is built around one promise:

children.value: your live site never goes down, and a broken build never reaches your visitors.

rows.value: You click deploy — or you simply publish content and Barkpark rebuilds on its own
No manual redeploy for content changes
Your site is built on separate infrastructure, reading your content over a private link
Your live site keeps serving the whole time
The new build is tested before anyone sees it
A broken build stops here — your current site is untouched
The instant the new build passes, visitors flip to it
The previous version is kept, ready to restore
If something's wrong, revert in one click, instantly

content.value: Change content in Barkpark and your site updates automatically — no redeploy, no waiting, no broken pages in between.
Because your site is built and served
, deploys are fast and updates are near-instant. There's nothing to wire up: spawn the site, and this pipeline is simply how it works.

blocks.text: What you can spawn today — and what's coming

content.value: Barkpark Cloud rolls these out in order of demand. Every framework plugs into the same engine, so the ones marked *coming* are add-ons on a shared foundation, not rewrites.

items.value: Astro (static) and Barkpark Native (instant).
Hugo — proving the same engine serves a second static framework with zero Node runtime.
Next.js and TanStack Start — server-rendered frameworks, once the secure per-site runtime lands.
SvelteKit, Nuxt, and Eleventy — filling out the menu.
for teams who want a global edge or a fully managed host, Barkpark can also deploy your site to an external platform instead of running it close to your content.

content.value: It covers the vast majority of sites beautifully, it's spawnable today, and nothing you build is wasted if you later graduate to a heavier framework.
*This guide is maintained by the Barkpark Cloud team. Framework capabilities and availability evolve — check your Cloud dashboard for the current menu when you spawn a site.*

Pluggable framework adapters — Astro first, the others slot into one engine.
A user-facing documentation guide meant to inform a real choice.

blocks.text: Epic cycle · design handoff spec
The Wave Deck — the epic cycle as an interactive, slide-by-slide experience

content.value: The 7-phase epic cycle already externalizes everything it knows into Barkpark — a living wave Paper, a published task ledger, a
wave_status

heartbeat. The Wave Deck renders that state as slides a human can ride: watch the fleet fly in realtime, see exactly what was checked and what wasn't, and DECIDE at five gates whether to research more, build, or land. This paper is the information spec: slide by slide, what each screen must inform, what is live, where the data already lives, and what is genuinely open for design.
This is the

spec for Claude design — content, data sources, decision moments, live elements. It deliberately says nothing about visual style, layout, or component aesthetics. Every slide below states its job in one line; if a slide can't, it shouldn't exist.

content.value: one glance answers “where is the wave, and how many minds are on it right now?” The current phase is lit; every gate shows whether it's upcoming, open (waiting on the user), or passed.

blocks.caption: The cycle with its five user gates. Every ↺ edge is a deliberate, cheap loop — research costs Sonnet minutes, not Opus hours.

blocks.text: The data contract — every slide, sourced

content.value: Nothing below requires a new backend write path. The cycle's liveness contract (heartbeat + stamp-as-you-go + Fable-owned Paper) was designed so any surface can render the wave from bp data plus the chat stream.

rows.value: epic task (flat fields), stamped by every Fable phase
workflow run + chat session (agents rail, drill-down)
synthesis, contradictions, verify plan w/ models

decisions, slice tasks, backlog, builder models

claim, criteria[] w/ evidence, lifecycle, stall notes

content.value: Today the 7 phases run as ONE background workflow. Real gates need the run to pause on user input. The clean cut: the workflow already externalizes ALL state into Paper + tasks at every Fable boundary — exactly where the gates sit. So gates = run the cycle as phase segments the lead fires one at a time (the deck's gate answer is the lead's cue), or a workflow-level pause primitive if one lands later. No phase needs to change what it writes.

blocks.text: Interaction doctrine

items.label: D1
items.lead: Gates are optional; auto mode is today's behavior.
items.text: Every gate has a default and (in auto) zero-wait pass-through. The deck adds decision power without taxing the user who trusts the loop.

items.label: D2
items.lead: Research loops are cheap by design.
items.text: “Research more” costs Sonnet-minutes. The deck shows the cost of each option AT the gate, so choosing more research feels safe, not indulgent.

items.label: D3
items.lead: Loops grow one Paper; they never fork.
items.text: Every extra round appends to the same wave Paper. The deck is a lens on the Paper — rewind any wave by scrolling it.

items.label: D4
items.text: Choice, author, note, timestamp — appended to the Paper. The wave's story includes the human's decisions, not just the agents'.

items.label: D5
items.lead: The wish never leaves the screen.
items.text: Every gate is judged against it. Persistent, verbatim, untruncated.

blocks.text: Principles the design must carry

items.label: P1
items.lead: Not-found is as loud as found.
items.text: Absence of prior art, a refuted premise, an unreached corner — these change plans. Never render them smaller than positives.

items.label: P2
items.lead: Always show what is in flight.
items.text: The Paper states the plan before each fleet flies; the deck must too. A mid-wave visitor orients in one glance.

items.label: P3
items.text: “14 agents” is a number; 14 cards with model badges, states, and assignments is a fleet. Aggregate AND enumerate.

items.label: P4
items.text: Grade travels with commentary; pass travels with the output that produced it; count travels with the list behind it.

items.label: P5
items.text: Agents die, gates go red, streams drop, builders stall. Each is a designed state, not an edge case — loading/empty/error at the Kinsta/Vercel bar.

items.label: P6
items.text: Every aggregate opens to its evidence: coverage cell → file+claim, proof row → full output, slice card → bp task, agent card → transcript.

items.label: P7
items.text: Deck states mirror task design language (open/claimed/in_progress/done, criteria met/unmet) — no parallel status taxonomy.

blocks.text: Open questions for Claude design

items.value: Deck vs scroll: are slides discrete steps (carousel with the loop map as navigator) or sections of one scrollable live document? The Paper is a scroll; the gates argue for steps.
Where do gate timeouts land — how long does a soft gate wait in attended mode before auto-defaulting, and how is that countdown shown?
Fleet view at 20 agents: cards, rows, or a swarm visualization with detail-on-hover? (80-col TUI parity exists as a constraint worth respecting — the deck should have a terminal projection someday.)
How does the deck coexist with the raw chat transcript — tabs, split, or the deck AS the chat's rich rendering of a wave-scoped session?
Multi-wave epics: does the deck show one wave or the epic's wave history (Paper per wave, charter as the spine)?
Notification surface for gates in unattended mode — push, email, Studio inbox (tickets exists), or all three?

blocks.text: The premise correction that sets this wave's shape

content.value: THE TRIAGE ALREADY EXISTS. The lead's brief says the 69 rows are "not vouched-for work; they are 69 rows that were somewhere else yesterday," and that our first job is triage. That was the right inference from the seal predicate — which reads only (_id, lifecycle_status, parent_id) and therefore cannot distinguish a chartered successor from a junk drawer. But it is falsified by reading the epic task itself. cloud-console-hardening-epic carries a ~9,000-character description containing a SIX-BAND disposition census that names all 69 rows individually, with a severity gradient inside Band 1, an explicit anti-bulk-forward rule ("THERE IS NO REST — these band lists are CLOSED"), a named first task, two inherited laws, and four acceptance criteria. A prior Fable spent round 10 of the seal doing exactly the triage we were told to do. The charter's own words: "THIS DESCRIPTION IS THE DIFFERENCE."

content.value: (A) THE REFETCH STORM — gr-blk-console-refetch-storm. The ONLY row in the entire roster carrying a live production measurement: on authenticated barkpark.cloud, five endpoints (/v1/barkparks, /v1/audit?limit=5, /v1/usage/summary, /v1/subscription, /v1/onboarding) were each requested EIGHT times in one page load — 40 requests where 5 would do — in seven evenly-spaced repeats consistent with one full reload per SSE event. Zero 4xx, zero 5xx, zero console errors, so no gate reds on it and it scales with SSE chatter. The client leg is one call site: cloud/priv/static/app.js:11919 opens the EventSource, and the invalidation handler around app.js:11789 is where a coarse {type} signal apparently triggers a blanket refetch. This is the highest-value row in the roster: real users, real cost, real latency, invisible to every instrument.

content.value: (B) COLLAPSED IDENTITY — gr-bl-peer-ip-container. The containerized control plane's Caddy hop arrives from the docker bridge gateway (172.18.0.1), and trust_forwarded_ip (router.ex:367) only calls RemoteIp when loopback_peer?(conn.remote_ip) is true — so it silently no-ops. TWO defects in one row, and the second is the serious one: every session row renders uniform garbage in the account UI, AND the device-auth `start:<ip>` rate bucket collapses to ONE GLOBAL BUCKET shared by every user, so a single abusive client throttles the entire platform. The fix must widen the trusted-peer predicate to the container gateway WITHOUT ever trusting an attacker-controlled X-Forwarded-For from a non-proxy peer — the existing comment at router.ex:365 states that invariant and it must survive.

content.value: (C) THE BEARER TOKEN IN THE URL — gr-blk-sse-token-in-query. Confirmed on BOTH legs: require_user_sse at router.ex:9705-9708 accepts a full session token via conn.query_params["token"], and app.js:11919 puts it there. A full-privilege, long-lived credential lands in access logs, proxy logs and browser history (CWE-598). DESIGN CONSTRAINT NAMED UP FRONT so a builder does not burn a round rediscovering it: the browser EventSource API cannot set an Authorization header, so "move it to a header" is NOT the fix. The fix is a short-TTL, single-use, SSE-scoped ticket minted by an authenticated POST and exchanged on connect.

content.value: 2. THE REFETCH STORM IS FULLY DE-RISKED, AND NARROWER THAN THE DIRECTION GUESSED. It is neither a blanket refetch nor N independent subscribers. TYPE_ACTIONS (app.js:12018-12061) is a closed, view-conditional dispatch table that behaves correctly for most event types. Exactly FOUR types — fleet, onboarding, barkpark.suspended, barkpark.restored — funnel through invalidateFleet (11970) and invalidateOnboarding (11995) into ONE shared monolith, loadOverview() (4847-4921), which unconditionally issues all five GETs on every call with zero awareness of which collection actually changed. There is no debounce, no dedupe, no in-flight guard, no AbortController anywhere in the 17k-line file. Cold boot calls loadOverview() exactly once (5 requests); seven SSE ticks add 35; total 40 — the production measurement, reproduced from code alone. Because the repeats are EVENLY SPACED, a time-window debounce would not suppress them: the fix must be scope-narrowing, not throttling. Falsifiable deterministically by a synthetic-event test counting fetch calls per type — no production access required. The second attack on this direction ('your flagship fix may be unfalsifiable') is answered.

content.value: 3. COLLAPSED IDENTITY: TOPOLOGY PROVEN, BLAST RADIUS PROVEN NARROW. Caddy runs on the HOST under systemd (not in docker-compose), reverse-proxying to 127.0.0.1:4100; cloud/docker-compose.yml publishes loopback-only with NO custom network, so Docker's hairpin-NAT rewrites every request's source to the default bridge gateway (172.18.0.1 observed live across all 19 real sessions and 17 days). loopback_peer? (router.ex:377-379) matches only 127.0.0.0/8 and ::1, so trust_forwarded_ip is a permanent no-op in production — precisely the failure the router's own comment at :243-245 predicted verbatim. The blast radius does NOT generalise: a full inventory of cloud/'s three rate-limiter modules and six call sites found EXACTLY ONE IP-keyed bucket (device-auth 'start:<ip>', 10 per 60s). poll keys on device_code_hash, approve and TFA key on user_id, test-email keys on team. So one predicate change repairs both stated defects and touches nothing else. The CI blind spot is confirmed: router_test.exs's 'front door' block tests {127,0,0,1} and {198,51,100,9} and never a bridge-gateway-shaped peer.

content.value: 4. THE HEAD SWEEP NEITHER COLLAPSED NOR EXPLODED — AND ITS SEVERITY WENT UP. All 56 block-form GET routes were enumerated and chased one level into their called modules. THREE side-effect, not one. The headline is a severity upgrade the direction did not anticipate: Plug.Head drops the response BODY, not the HEADERS, and redirect_to (router.ex:9587-9591) puts the freshly-minted session token in the Location header. A HEAD probe against a still-valid oauth callback URL therefore receives a live session token in cleartext — credential exfiltration, not merely a burned nonce. Separately, the flow INITIATOR (GET /v1/auth/oauth/:provider, router.ex:876) Repo.insert!s a fresh oauth_states row on every unauthenticated hit, and no prune job for that table exists anywhere in cloud/lib — unbounded growth under repeated probing. The third route (GET /v1/notifications/settings) writes a default EmailSettings row on first call: real, idempotent, low severity. gr-blk-oauth-head-mint's own acceptance criterion 3 — 'the remaining 55 GET routes are confirmed side-effect-free' — is now known FALSE.

content.value: 5. THE CSSOM-PARITY GATE IS MUTATION-PROVEN TODAY, AND ITS WIRING HAS ONE HARD BLOCKER NOBODY HAD NAMED. The instrument merged in PR #4830 (1ca6ff4a3) and is referenced by ZERO of the 34 workflow files. A surveyor re-ran the mutation proof twice, live, on an app.css byte-identical to origin/main (sha256 bdd60416…): stripping the comment opener at line 1040 produced MISSES 2, exit 1, naming .modal-root at :1045; the same mutation class at :3122 produced MISSES 1, naming .wh-secret at :3123 — 2,000 lines away, proving the check is file-wide. Both restored byte-clean. NOTE that the line numbers stamped as evidence on the original task (:1029/:1034, :3076/:3077) are already stale — app.css moves every wave, so no CI step or doc may hardcode them. THE BLOCKER: cssom-parity.mjs calls bare global `new WebSocket()` with no import or polyfill, and console-harness.yml pins node-version: 20, where that global is not enabled by default. A naive fourth step appended to the existing job throws ReferenceError before ever reaching Chrome — shipping a red gate on day one, which is the single worst outcome for a brand-new browser-backed check.

content.value: 6. ALL THREE LYING HARNESSES CONFIRMED, AND TWO OF THEM ARE ONE DELIVERABLE. scenarios.mjs has a GET handler for /v1/account/sessions but NO DELETE handler for it or its :id form; both fall to the generic catch-all at line 3051 returning 200 {}, so app.js:1007 renders the literal toast '0 session(s) revoked.' emit.mjs's evaluate() splices freshly-built content over whatever sat between the BEGIN/END markers with no diff and no warning, and check.mjs imports that same evaluate() — so after a --write, current and expected are byte-identical BY CONSTRUCTION and check.mjs prints PASS regardless of what was deleted (precedent: 33 hand-written rules deleted in 1d928b3bf). smoke.mjs's DOM shim declares addEventListener(){}, click(){} and querySelectorAll(){return []} as literal no-ops, and says so in its own header. THE COUPLING, which Decide must not miss: revoke-harness-gap's criterion 2 ('clicks Revoke… asserts the correct DELETE path was hit') and click-inert's criterion 2 ('at least one consequential wire proven by a machine click') are the SAME deliverable. They cannot be filed as independent slices.

content.value: CORRECTION 1 — THE SSE TICKET IS NOT FREE, AND THIS IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT NEW FACT. The direction named the constraint 'EventSource cannot set headers, so a header is NOT the fix — mint a short-TTL single-use SSE-scoped ticket.' The first half is right. The second half hides an architectural tension the survey exposed: EventSource freezes its URL at construction (app.js:11919), and the client's onerror handler (11943-11954) only toasts and repaints the liveness chip — it never closes or reopens the stream. Native browser reconnect therefore replays the SAME frozen URL forever. A literal single-use ticket means the first connection consumes it and EVERY subsequent native retry 401s permanently — a regression strictly worse than the leak being fixed, and it would fail the task's own criterion 2 on any network flap. There are exactly two honest resolutions: (a) ship short-TTL MULTI-connect and name it that, never overselling it as single-use; or (b) ship true single-use AND rewrite the client reconnect path — close, mint over a bearer header, reconstruct EventSource, add explicit backoff to avoid a mint storm, and extend the liveness state machine to model an app-driven remint gap. This is a DECIDE-TIME RULING, not a builder detail. The mechanism itself needs no migration: user_tokens.context is an unconstrained string column, 2fa_pending is the short-TTL mint template, and reset_password_by_token is the battle-tested single-use consume-in-transaction template.

content.value: SSE TICKET SEMANTICS (V1, headless Chrome over CDP). The question was framed one notch too narrow. Proven: EventSource freezes its URL at construction and replays it byte-identically — 12 requests across 3 runs, all identical. And the decisive new fact nobody had: ANY 401 is TERMINAL. Measured, always401 run: 'REQUESTS TO /v1/events: 1 … CLIENT EVENTS (1): + 2106ms error 2' — one request, readyState 2, zero retries over 15s. So short-TTL multi-connect does NOT avoid the cliff; it shares it on TTL expiry. The client change is mandatory under BOTH designs.

(2) The refetch storm has a FIFTH, open-ended trigger (the barkpark.* prefix fallback) — enumerating four types leaves it storming. (3) The HEAD sweep is 2 routes, not 3, and 2 is a FLOOR not a ceiling (the body-scan method would have missed the initiator's own one-call-deep write). (4) gr-blk-oauth-head-mint's criterion 3 ('the remaining 55 GET routes are confirmed side-effect-free') is now known FALSE.

content.value: D11-D16 — the HEAD fix is a router-level deny-list plug placed BEFORE plug(Plug.Head), because Plug.Head destroys HEAD-ness with no stash so per-route short-circuits are impossible rather than merely inferior; it answers 405 with allow: GET, because 404 is the lie #4481 was landed to remove; it is a deny-list not opt-in tagging, because opt-in inverts the default so a forgotten new route silently 404s again; it matches on path_info segment lists, because path_params are unpopulated at plug time; it prunes oauth_states, because no reaper exists and both legs insert per unauthenticated hit; and it is framed as a response-header leak, not CWE-598, because the token rides the fragment.

content.value: What falls short, honestly. The peer-IP fix is unproven above unit level and, worse, cannot be proven until a human recreates the compose network — a merge could abort the auto-deploy into its safe-failure path and nothing would land. The refetch slice's harness is a fake DOM that models node identity and innerHTML destruction but does not parse markup or run listeners, so the claim that the rebuilt grid renders correctly in a browser is inspection, not execution. The emit fence still has a side door (paper-editor-mirror.mjs writes the mirror region directly, bypassing emit.mjs entirely) and its manifest will conflict on merge whenever two branches touch tokens.json, with --force sitting right there as the reflex. The cssom floor is a static absolute whose sensitivity decays as app.css grows. All four are FILED, none are hidden — which is why this is A minus and not B plus.

content.value: So on the merged tree: HEAD /v1/events?ticket=X passes the deny-list (not side-effecting), Plug.Head rewrites HEAD to GET unconditionally before matching, the route runs, and the ticket is BURNED - by a request that returns no body. Any honest prober, unfurler, uptime monitor or proxy that HEADs the stream URL destroys a live user's credential; under D10's mandatory remint the client remints and reopens, so the failure mode is a burn/remint loop with one 401 per iteration - exactly the access-log noise D10 exists to prevent.

content.value: The law this wave proposes (D41, for Decide to ratify or refute)

blocks.text: The law this wave proposes (D41, for Decide to ratify or refute)

content.value: D40 ratified: every enforcement mechanism states its own coverage boundary. This wave's evidence says that is necessary and NOT sufficient. The HEAD deny-list DID state its boundary, explicitly and well ('Out of scope BY DECISION. Do not grow this list'), and the boundary became false two commits later inside the same wave. Proposed D41: a coverage boundary must be MACHINE-CHECKED, not merely documented - an enforcement mechanism that can silently go stale needs a tripwire that reds when the world moves out from under it, and a comment is not a tripwire. The head-denylist tripwire and the __css_check states boundary are its first two payments, and both are already filed rows.

content.value: The epic is ~90% security and instrument hygiene. A console that does not lie is table stakes; the premium bar is FEEL - destructive confirms, honest empty states, the liveness chip reading right, a silently-failing background refresh becoming visible. Build revoke-ux-honesty plus the two Overview honesty rows plus the chip polish. Genuinely tempting, and it owns the one quality dimension the epic keeps deferring. Wave 4 is the right home for a UX-led wave, once the security thread is closed.

content.value: ATTACK: the HEAD-burns-ticket defect may be near-unexploitable, and the mint rate-limit may be a phantom. If both rows are low-severity, the wave has built its direction on two shrugs and Rival A was right.

content.value: ABSORPTION, three ways. First, severity is not the argument - PROVENANCE is. Even at low severity the finding is the best available proof of D41, because it is an accepted risk that fired inside the wave that accepted it, and that is worth building the tripwire for regardless of the instance's CVSS. Second, the honest-prober path needs no attacker at all: a monitor or unfurler HEADing the stream URL is a plain availability and log-noise defect on a real user's session. Third, the wave does not ASSUME severity - it measures it. The survey is instructed to establish whether the mint inserts an unreaped row per call (making it D15's exact sibling and clearly real) or whether some existing reaper covers context="sse" (making it noise), and to establish who actually issues HEAD against the console. If the measurement says phantom, Decide drops the row and the wave keeps the tripwire, which is the part that carries the law.

content.value: THE HEAD-BURNS-TICKET DEFECT IS CONFIRMED BY CONTENT, NOT YET BY EXECUTION. Full trace on the composed tree: refuse_head_on_side_effecting_gets runs at router.ex:303 with side_effecting_get?/1 fencing exactly two oauth paths plus a catch-all false (router.ex:479-489), so [v1, events] falls through; Plug.Head at router.ex:305 rewrites the method to GET and stashes nothing; the get /v1/events handler calls require_user_sse, which falls through to conn.query_params[ticket] and then Accounts.consume_sse_ticket(ticket); and consume_sse_ticket/1 (accounts.ex:2047) takes a bare binary, locks FOR UPDATE and stamps revoked_at unconditionally, structurally incapable of knowing the HTTP method. No HEAD test against /v1/events exists in either slice's test file - every HEAD test in router_sse_ticket_test.exs targets the mint route. The defect was invisible to both builders because each was inside its own fence. Adding side_effecting_get?([v1, events]) is sufficient AND architecturally correct: the plug is unconditional, runs before Plug.Head (so it still sees the true method) and before route dispatch, and matches path segments only. Threading a conn into Accounts would break the layering both slices otherwise preserve.

content.value: THE MINT ROW-GROWTH ROW IS REAL, AND ITS SHAPE IS A REAPER, NOT A THROTTLE. create_sse_ticket/1 does a bare Repo.insert of a context=sse user_tokens row per call, explicitly non-superseding by its own docstring; consume_sse_ticket only soft-marks revoked_at, never deletes; POST /v1/auth/sse-ticket carries only Auth.require_user with no rate-limit plug, while TwoFactorRateLimiter and DeviceAuthRateLimiter guard sibling routes six lines away in the same file; and a grep across cloud/lib/barkpark_cloud/workers/ for UserToken returns nothing at all - no worker touches user_tokens by any context. The precedent is exact and doubled: device_auth_reaper.ex is on main today, and oauth_state_reaper.ex (D15's own payment) is a new file on PR #5378 with the identical shape. Since the caller must already hold a valid session the blast radius is bounded, which makes the reaper the better-precedented, lower-risk shape; the task's own criteria leave throttle-versus-prune open.

content.value: THE CSS CLASS IS SMALLER THAN THE DIRECTION THOUGHT, AND THE CHEAP FIX MAY NOT LIVE IN __css_check AT ALL. There are FOUR setAttribute data-* sites in app.js, not three: :3312 data-theme, :3344 data-bp-theme, :11871 data-state, and :16178 data-theme inside coherenceStampTheme - a second theme emitter the direction's recon missed. But three of the four are NOT uncovered: E5, the contrast engine at __css_check.mjs:636-679, parses the data-theme and data-bp-theme blocks straight out of app.css and fans every combination through WCAG. Exactly ONE attribute name (data-state) from exactly ONE emission site is genuinely unchecked, fed by exactly ONE six-line pure function, liveDotState (app.js:11816-11821, three literal returns - live, stale, reconnecting), which is ALREADY exported via hooks.liveDotState and unit-tested at __app.test.mjs:4006-4029. cssom-parity.mjs has zero data-state references and is structurally blind (it diffs CSS against CSSOM and never reads app.js). So the honest fix may be a mutation-provable assertion in __app.test.mjs over liveDotState's literal return set, rather than teaching E2's literal-string regex to read attribute values that are always variables. Both are cheap; the choice is real and should be made with a run, not a preference.

content.value: THE TRIPWIRE IS THE WAVE'S ONLY GENUINELY HARD SLICE, AND THE DIRECTION UNDERSOLD IT. The census-with-a-floor precedent exists - router_moduledoc_table_test.exs regex-extracts every route declaration and diffs it against the moduledoc table in both directions, guarded by a >100 vacuous-green floor - but it extracts single DECLARATION LINES. This tripwire needs BODY text, and a surveyor who actually tried indent-based end-matching on the live router got implausible results (it flagged /v1/me and /v1/audit as unauthenticated) because nested do/end/case/cond/fn defeat naive counting. There is NO first-party Elixir AST precedent anywhere in cloud/ (Code.string_to_quoted and Macro.prewalk hit only deps/) and no .credo.exs to hang a custom check on. Meanwhile a literal Repo. call appears inside get blocks roughly ONCE across all ~56 clauses - so one-call-deep is load-bearing, not decorative, and satisfying it means either an AST walk or a hardcoded manifest of write-bearing helper names, which is itself an ignore-list that goes stale exactly like the deny-list it polices.

content.value: THE ORACLE COLLISION IS REAL BUT NARROW, AND IT HAS A ONE-LINE REMEDY. Only ONE leg of one scenario is at risk: cch-w2-revoke-ux-honesty's AC2 gates a confirmModal on revoke-all only; per-row Revoke gets a toast plus a pending state and its DELETE still fires on the same click. Once #sessions-revoke-all wraps its api(DELETE) in openConfirmModal, smoke.mjs:539-559's countCalls assertion reads 0 and everything after it dies. The oracle CAN drive it: the app's own selector and the test's registry lookup resolve through the same byId Map singleton, and at DANGER tier (the 2FA-disable precedent at app.js:960) confirmModalArmed returns true immediately - one extra click. At DESTROY tier the oracle must also set the typed-echo field and dispatch input, materially more. Two hazards Decide must fence: (a) a harness FIDELITY GAP - openModal replaces the modal body wholesale in a real browser, but the shim's flat parser only recognises button and a tags and #sessions-box is an independent registry singleton, so a post-confirm session-list assertion can pass in the shim while the real browser shows a closed modal, unless onConfirm re-renders the way app.js:975 does; and (b) none of the ux-honesty ACs say edit account-modal-revoke IN PLACE, do not duplicate, so a builder could leave the existing scenario permanently red on merge.

content.value: DEBRIEF — what shipped, what it cost, the grade, and what the next wave takes

One reviewer, last hands before merge. Every gate was RE-RUN on the reviewer's own tree rather than taken on report, every load-bearing claim was re-proven by an independent mutation, and every issue found was FIXED in place on a -r branch rather than written up. All six slices are green, and all six -r branches merge into origin/main with zero conflicts in any order.
Composite proof, on the integrated merge of all six -r branches

This is Act 3, and it is not a promise — it was run. cloud 'mix test' 2199 tests / 0 failures (2182 baseline + 6 head-burn + 4 census + 7 reaper, so the delta is exactly the new files and no collateral skip hid behind a green); api targeted suite 1325 / 0; smoke.mjs all 87 scenarios rendered; __app.test.mjs 661 / 661; __css_check 0 errors; pr-task-gate.test.sh passed 32 failed 0; and 'mix format --check-formatted' clean on every touched Elixir file. The head-burn test is now a standing gate with zero CI wiring, exactly as D62/Act 3 predicted: cloud.yml's bare 'mix test' picks it up.
Per slice — final branch and verdict

cch-bl-head-denylist-tripwire -> loop-epic/head-stops-burning-a-live-sse-ticket-the-0-r (afcf40751). The wave's best slice. One fence clause closes a defect proven by RUN in both directions; the census pin is honest about its own narrow marginal value (D57) rather than oversold. Reviewer fixes: the classifier now strips comment-only lines so a route that merely NAMES a wrapper in prose cannot pass as authenticated (mutation-killed both ways; the census stays byte-identical at 62/45/5/12), the D40 block names the class-SWAP hole outright, and the number-word table flunks with instructions instead of raising KeyError. Independently mutation-killed: removing the deny clause reds 7 of 10.

cch-bl-sse-ticket-mint-rate-limit -> loop-epic/the-sse-ticket-table-gets-a-reaper-burne-1-r (43a985fea). A reaper, not a throttle, per D48, with the rejected alternative argued in the moduledoc. Reviewer fixes: the NULL-expires_at survivor case is PINNED rather than reasoned (a NULL-eager WHERE reds it), and the moduledoc now states the cost its twins do not carry — it sweeps the SHARED user_tokens with no context-leading index, so each tick is a seq scan plus an unbounded DELETE, with the revisit condition written down.

cch-bl-css-check-states-boundary -> loop-epic/css-check-e2-declares-its-own-coverage-b-2-r (7cde45b0f). Comment-only by design, and it buys nothing executable — the builder said so first, which is the point. Reviewer found a REAL defect: the block pinned five app.js line numbers that its own sibling slice shifts +39. Re-anchored to enclosing function names plus the regenerating grep. Both documented mutations independently re-reproduced.

cch-w2-ledger-close-guard-create-ops -> loop-epic/the-ledger-s-claim-survives-every-door-a-3-r (5d4ab6650). The largest and the most consequential: a separate orthogonal claim fence at all four doors, D50's trap avoided (replace's with-chain untouched, its 404 now pinned), D52's three siblings closed plus a fourth found in self-review. Reviewer fix: round 1's terminal-status drift tripwire swept only the PATCH door while this slice widened the guard to four — it now sweeps all three, mutation-killed. Independently mutation-killed both guards (claim fence off: 8 of 34 red; close guard off at createOrReplace only: 4 of 34 red).

cch-w2-revoke-ux-honesty -> loop-epic/destructive-session-controls-confirm-and-4-r (90296fec1). The one user-facing slice, and it clears the Kinsta/Vercel bar: danger-tier confirm on the blast-radius button with a working retry arm, pending state plus success toast on the per-row leg, and a mandatory re-render whose necessity is explained in code. Both decisive mutation kills independently re-reproduced. Reviewer fix: the coverage-boundary block refreshed the four citations beside its own edit and left SIX further down stale by the same shift; all are now named by route.

cch-bl-pr-task-gate-backtick-regex -> MERGED as #5439 (e23951203) mid-review; follow-up on loop-epic/pr-task-gate-accepts-a-backtick-wrapped--5-r (92ae6f847, cut fresh on origin/main). The smallest slice with the largest structural honesty: it moved the grammar out of YAML into a script the hermetic harness can reach, which is why it was untestable for months. Reviewer fixes: CRLF cases pinned and mutation-killed, and the harness's failure printer switched to %q — the CRLF mutation printed 'want cch-bl-x got cch-bl-x', a diagnostic that lied about its own defect.
What stalled

Nothing. Zero slices stalled, zero came back BLOCKED, and every precondition verified by content on current origin/main at review time. The only surprise was directional rather than a stall: slice 6 merged as #5439 while review was in flight, so its -r follow-up had to be re-cut on origin/main — D59's point (state is point-in-time; re-read before every mutating call) firing one more time.
The grade: A-

GENUINELY STRONG. The wave did what its own frame demands and did it to itself. Four filed criteria were refuted by measurement and rewritten rather than built, and the builders kept doing it: slice 1 found that this charter's D34 wrapper list does not reproduce its own numbers (the 8 named wrappers give 40/5/17, not 45/5/12) and filed a correction row instead of quietly patching the classifier; slice 4 found a FOURTH open patch sibling in self-review after D52 named three; slice 3 re-measured the attribute population and found FIVE where the brief said four. Every builder's own review section reads like an adversary's, naming the judgement calls (the :sync exemption, the counts-not-sets pin, the unmeasured theft-by-overwrite hole) instead of burying them. The proofs are mutation-killed in both directions, not merely green. Seven follow-up rows were filed published mid-build. That is the epic's predicate turned on the epic, sustained across six independent agents.

WHAT FALLS SHORT, and why it is a minus rather than a plus. Three separate stale-source-citation defects shipped in one wave — one slice pinned line numbers its own sibling invalidated, one refreshed four citations and left six, and one pre-existing citation had already rotted. That is D41's disease, in the wave that MINTED D41, and no builder caught it because each looked only at its own file. It cost the reviewer three fixes and earned a new row. Second, the census pin is counts and not sets, so a same-commit class swap passes — defensible under bp-honest-gates D5/D11 and now stated outright, but a real hole in a slice sold as a drift ceiling. Third, the wave's own residual harms are named and unclosed by construction: claim theft-by-OVERWRITE was filed with 'MEASURE FIRST' as its first criterion because the builder honestly did not run the probe, and the forged-fresh-create -> Tasks.Queue.ready hole has no compensating control. Fourth, one slice (css-check boundary) is 63 lines of comment that changes no gate behaviour — correct per D49, and the builder said so plainly, but it is the wave's thinnest deliverable. Nothing here is bloat and nothing is wrong; the gap between this and an A is that the wave proved its own law and then broke it three times.
Ledger audit

Clean, and the best this epic has produced. All six slice tasks sit in_progress — not one false 'done' — with every non-merge-gated criterion stamped and carrying quoted run output, all six parented to cloud-console-hardening-epic and linked to this Paper, all six with a live claim. The merge-gated criterion is UNMET on every one, correctly left for the lead (standing law 5). Seven follow-ups were filed published by the builders mid-build: cch-bl-d34-wrapper-list-correction, cch-bl-lifecycle-token-reaper, cch-bl-state-rule-per-declaration-gate, cch-w3-task-birth-attribution, cch-w3-claim-overwrite-fence, cch-bl-smoke-shim-fidelity, cch-bl-reland-check-backtick-trailer. No task outside the wave was touched. Review added one row, cch-bl-source-citation-line-drift, and pulsed all six slice now-lines with the verdict and the branch to merge.
What the lead must know before merging
Merge the -r branches, not the originals — every one carries reviewer fixes. Slice 6 is already on main (#5439); merge only its -r follow-up.
The merge-gated criterion on all six is the LEAD's to close, by MERGE SHA, never a branch SHA (standing law 1 and 5). Slice 6's is closable NOW with e23951203.
Also merge loop-epic/cch-wave-3-review-charter — the wave-log entry, cut clean off origin/main.

Two behaviour changes ride out in the open and are intended, not incidental. HEAD /v1/events now answers 405 instead of opening a stream (D43: no first-party consumer HEADs this console, so this is preventive). And 'blocked' is terminal, so createOrReplace/replace now require an ifRevisionID for it — which makes the create-family doors agree with the patch door.

Sign-out-everywhere now sends { noBounce: true }, so an expired token renders inline in the confirm sheet instead of bouncing to login. That is the confirmModal failure contract and the 2FA-disable precedent, but it IS a change in what a 401 does on that button.

The SSE reaper's first production tick deletes every burned/expired sse row accumulated since #5377 in one unbounded statement. The table is days old so the batch is small, but nobody measured the live row count.
What the next wave takes

This wave paid the class at three doors and NAMED two holes it could not close. The next wave closes the named ones first — that is the sequenced-rounds law applied to residue rather than to files. In order: (1) cch-w3-claim-overwrite-fence, claim theft-by-OVERWRITE, whose first criterion is literally 'MEASURE FIRST' and is unrun — it is the largest remaining hole in the class slice 4 claims to have paid; (2) cch-w3-task-birth-attribution, the forged-fresh-create -> Tasks.Queue.ready hole, the one residual harm this wave measured and left standing; (3) cch-bl-source-citation-line-drift, because three occurrences in one wave is a class, and D41 says a class is paid with a ratchet and not with prose; (4) cch-bl-d34-wrapper-list-correction, because this charter's own D34 does not reproduce its own numbers and a builder had to correct it silently in code to make the census work. cch-bl-smoke-shim-fidelity is the stretch row: the shim's flat registry can still manufacture the D55 false green in a NEW place, and slice 5's fix was discipline, not mechanism.

content.value: The inspector stops borrowing the reader's column — the desk pays for it in priority order

Living wave Paper for the FIRST wave of `spd-b39-user-opened-inspector-shape-successor`, which stands as its OWN ROOT work. Its parent epic `studio-space-priority-desk` CLOSED at wave-9 Review on D136 with a refused seal — NO SEAL argued separately on three ledgers (D136 i/ii/iii) — and D142 moved this successor to root rather than keeping a dead epic open as a container. Charter: `.claude/workflows/bp-studio-space-priority-charter.md`, D1-D147.

READING DISCIPLINE, inherited and load-bearing. Every code fact in this Paper was read via `git show origin/main:<path>`. The primary checkout is 100 commits BEHIND origin/main and 13 commits AHEAD of it (it carries the wave-9 amendment D136-D147, which origin does not) — so neither tree alone is the truth, and a grep of the working copy returns CONFIDENT EMPTY results that manufactured two overturns in the parent epic. Code from origin/main; charter ledger from the local file; every desk number from the committed artifact `scripts/measurements/spd-visible-table-2026-07-20.json` at origin/main, served SHA `65541e2d43e7ea116c6d49e0ac0b1e0109c93a8f`, slot blue, provenance bracket matched, 54 rows, non-vacuity guard applied in 21 of 21 applicable rows, `unsettled_rows` 0.

STATUS: Strategize complete — the wave is SURVEYING. Digest appends the survey digest and the verify plan BEFORE the verifiers fly; Decide appends the decisions and the wave plan BEFORE the builders fly; Review closes this Paper as the debrief. Per the model constraint, every slice dispatches with `builder_model: opus`. No phase of this wave runs on Fable.
The wish

Decide the shape of the user-summoned inspector, ship it, and MEASURE it with the committed instrument against the DEPLOYED build. The question is explicitly NOT 'dock or overlay' — D126 killed that framing with arithmetic. The real question, pre-registered by D127 and handed over undecided: is a user-summoned inspector a MODE in which the reading bar is deliberately suspended AND SAID to be — or is the reading bar law, meaning the panel may never take the screen and must become something else entirely?

D127 is explicit about ORDER, not about the answer: the successor MAY rule the mode exempt, but only after stating the rule BEFORE it looks at its own table. This Paper states that rule below, in the Direction section, written against a table that already exists and is already public — so the pre-registration is about the SUCCESSOR's table, the one the shape this wave ships will produce.
What we inherit, measured rather than argued

The committed 54-row table is the ground. 9 viewport widths x 3 forced faces x 2 inspector states. D107 fixed 'desktop rows' BEFORE any table was consulted: 1440, 1280, 1024, 900, 800, 764, 700. Viewport 640 is an excluded named shortfall; viewport 500 / phone was never ch-gated (its criterion is navigability plus no horizontal scroll).

THE DEFAULT STATE IS A LARGE, REAL WIN. `spd-b29` shipped the D91 hybrid: below the `wide` bucket the cascade paints the never-asked-for inspector as a 41px in-flow strip, and the scrim is suppressed there (0 of 27 default rows render it). Default-state visible reading width, resolved Iowan face, probe 10.0000 px/ch at 18px: 1440 640px / 1280 596px / 1024 599px / 900 640px / 800 635px / 764 631px / 700 567px. Eighteen of the twenty-one desktop default cells MEET >=55ch. Three refuse, ALL forced Georgia (11.0469 px/ch at 18px): 1280 at 53.95ch, 1024 at 54.22ch, 700 at 51.33ch — `overflow_px: 0` in all three, genuinely narrow columns rather than scroll-masked ones. D141 restated their ownership BY MECHANISM: the 720px surface cap plus Georgia's advance, owned by `spd-b42-georgia-default-shortfall-inflow-width`, NOT by a floor bind and NOT by `spd-b28` (which is `done` and whose own close reason disclaims them).

THE USER-OPENED STATE IS THE DEFECT, AND IT IS TOTAL BELOW `wide`. Quoted from `visible_meets_55ch`, never `content_meets_55ch` (D139 — the two fields disagree by FIFTEEN on the 21 desktop user-opened cells, and quoting the layout field would let a ruling claim 20-of-21 MEET in the very state it is refusing). The honest ledger is 5 MEET, 16 FAIL. All five MEETs sit in the `wide` bucket where the inspector DOCKS: `position: static`, `overlap_over_content_box_px: 0`, scrim absent, one-click delta 0.000px. Sub-wide, at 1024 / 900 / 800 / 764 / 700 x three faces, it is 15 of 15 FAIL without exception. The sixteen failures decompose and must be quoted decomposed: THIRTEEN are overlay-caused (MEET in default, FAIL on one click) and THREE are inherited from the default shortfall and fail in both states.

THE SHARPEST CELL. At a 1024px viewport on the resolved Iowan face, one click takes the reader from 599.000px = 59.90ch to 378.958px = 37.90ch. 220.042px = 22.00ch gone, with the inspector at `position: absolute`, `width: 300px`, overlapping the content box by 260px. D109 names what makes this a DEFECT rather than a disliked number: at that same click the LAYOUT metric RISES (`content_px` 599 -> 640, because the 41px strip leaves flow and hands its width back to the panel) while the reader LOSES 219px. The layout number and the human move in opposite directions on the single interaction this work is about.

AND IT IS A HALF-STATE, NOT A MODE. The scrim covers the ENTIRE content box at 55% black (`scrim_covers_content_fully: true`, `scrim_alpha: 0.55`, `dimmed_content_px` equal to the row's whole `visible_content_px` in each of the 21 rows where it renders). The text is dimmed, not hidden. And the reader cannot leave: `spd-b12-inspector-overlay-dismiss` is open at 0/4 — no Escape, no tap-to-dismiss, no `aria-modal`, no focus management — and the scrim is a `::after` PSEUDO-ELEMENT carrying `pointer-events: none` by deliberate design (a click-catching scrim would swallow edits), so it structurally cannot carry a dismiss handler. Neither a clean mode nor a viable dock. That indeterminacy is D127's real subject.

THE CEILING, AS THE CHARTER LEFT IT. D126: `ceiling = min(panel_px, surface cap 720) - gutter - 55 x probe px/ch`. At 1024 that is 90.0px on the resolved Iowan face, 32.4px forced Georgia, 135.5px Source Serif 4 — and it is FLAT from 800 through 1440, because the 720px surface cap binds at every width at or above 1024. A metadata panel does not fit in 90px. The corrected in-flow comparable is 340px = 34.00ch; the 420px / ~42ch figure is STRUCK by D126 and may not be quoted.
The finding that reopens the option set

D126's arithmetic, and the criterion-2 evidence string on `spd-b39` that repeats it, hold `panel_px` FIXED at its measured 720 at viewport 1024. But 720 is not a constraint — it is a CHOICE the desk is currently making. The committed artifact records the pane rail per row: at 1024 it is `visible_pane_widths_px: [44, 260]`. The desk is spending 260px on a document-list column while it overlays the inspector on the prose. 1024 = 44 + 260 + 720.

The parent epic's own Vision sentence declares the priority order that was never run at this transition, verbatim: 'all squeeze flows outward by explicit priority (list pane compresses first, then rails to 44px strips, then the Document inspector overlays instead of docking)'. At 1024 the list pane has never been asked to compress. The inspector goes straight to the overlay — step three of a ladder whose first step was skipped.

The machinery to run it ALREADY SHIPS. `BarkparkWeb.Studio.PaneBuilder.display_state/4` returns `:full | :strip | :hidden` per pane. In the `narrow` bucket with an editor open, every pane is `:hidden` except the LAST, which is a 44px `:strip` — which is exactly why the artifact reads `[44]` at 900 and below and `[44, 260]` at 1024, where the `standard` branch instead returns `:strip` iff `collapse?/3` else `:full`. The rule that frees the pixels is written, tested and deployed; it is simply not reachable from the `standard` bucket, and nothing in the codebase lets the inspector's own state influence it.

RUN THE LADDER AT 1024, on measured inputs. If opening the inspector applies the shipped `narrow` rule, the rail goes [44, 260] -> [44] and the panel goes 720 -> 980. Dock the 300px inspector in flow: surface = min(680, 720) = 680; the gutter READ at 1024 in the committed artifact is 80px total; content = 600px. Per face, each divided by its OWN probe advance at 18px, no cross-face division: 600 / 10.0000 = 60.00ch resolved Iowan; 600 / 11.0469 = 54.31ch forced Georgia; 600 / 9.1719 = 65.42ch forced Source Serif 4.

Read that against what ships today at the same cell: 37.90 / 34.30 / 41.32ch. The reader who opens the inspector at 1024 would end up with MORE reading width than they had before opening it (default is 599px = 59.90ch), with the inspector DOCKED, `overlap_over_content_box_px: 0`, and the scrim never rendering. Forced Georgia lands at 54.31ch — which is the INHERITED default shortfall (54.22ch at that same width) essentially unchanged, owned by `spd-b42-georgia-default-shortfall-inflow-width`, and NOT overlay-caused. Charging it to the inspector would double-count the default shortfall, which D139 forbids by name.

This arithmetic is a HYPOTHESIS, stated so it can fail. It rests on four assumptions this wave must break or confirm before it builds: that the `standard` bucket's second pane can be driven to `:hidden` by an inspector-state input at all; that the panel actually claims the freed width rather than something else absorbing it; that the 80px gutter reading at 1024 survives the panel change; and that a 300px in-flow inspector inside a 980px panel does not trip horizontal overflow on `.editor-body.bp-paper-body`. Each is a survey and verify assignment below.
The direction

THE INSPECTOR STOPS BORROWING THE READER'S COLUMN, AND THE DESK PAYS FOR IT IN PRIORITY ORDER. The answer to D127's binary is neither horn alone: the reading bar is LAW at every width where the desk can still pay for the inspector out of lower-priority space, and it is SUSPENDED-AND-SAID only where a run proves there was nothing left to sell. A three-tier ladder, each tier chosen by arithmetic rather than by taste.

TIER 1 — `wide` (1280, 1440). UNCHANGED, and this is a hard constraint rather than an omission. The inspector docks, costs 0.000px on the click, `visible_content_px == content_px`, and five of the six MEETs in the entire user-opened table live here. Any slice this wave dispatches must prove wide moved zero pixels, by the runtime rule-deletion diff D102 used, not by assertion.

TIER 2 — `standard` (1024). THE LIST YIELDS AND THE INSPECTOR DOCKS. On the click that opens the inspector, the desk applies the pane rule it already ships one bucket down; the 260px document-list column folds to nothing (its 44px strip stays on screen and clickable, the same distinction `spd-b29` proved is the difference between a collapsed strip and an un-openable panel), the panel takes the width, and the inspector sits BESIDE the prose instead of on top of it. No overlay. No scrim. No mode. The >=55ch bar HOLDS here and is measured, not exempted. This is the wave's headline, and it converts the single sharpest cell in the whole ledger from 37.90ch to a predicted 60.00ch.

TIER 3 — `narrow` and `phone` (900 and below). THE PANEL STOPS BEING A PANEL. Here the arithmetic is genuinely closed and the charter is right: D113 measured that `.editor-panel`'s left edge is 44px at EVERY sub-wide width — the rail has already yielded everything, there is nothing left to sell — and docking is not merely insufficient but WORSE than the overlay at 800 (a 300px dock inside a 756px panel leaves 376px of content against the overlay's measured 396.9px). So the inspector becomes a SUMMONED DESTINATION: it takes the whole panel, the reading column is LEFT rather than dimmed, and the breadcrumb drill that ALREADY SHIPS at `phone` (the artifact records `crumbs.host_present: true`, `visible: true`, `count: 3` at viewport 500, with `pane_columns: 0`) carries the reader back. This is Sanity's shape, MD3's standard-sheet tier, and the parent epic's own vision sentence for phone, extended upward to every width where docking is dead.

THE UNIFYING RULE, and the aesthetic core: NOWHERE does the desk end up with a reader's prose at 55% black under a panel. The dimming is ABOLISHED, not tuned. A mode either shows the document or it does not, and the shipped design's refusal to choose is the defect D127 is really asking about. Pay for the dock where the desk can afford it; leave the document where it cannot.
The pre-registered rule (D127), stated before the successor's table is consulted

This is written now, in a published Paper, before this wave's shape exists and therefore before its table exists. It will be landed as a numbered decision in the charter FILE in the same wave that cites it (D135), because a Paper's claim to have committed something is a claim like any other and this work verifies claims.

RULE, part 1 — WHERE THE BAR APPLIES. In the user-opened state the >=55ch bar APPLIES at every width where a reading column is on screen: `wide` and `standard`. It is measured there by `visible_meets_55ch` (D139), per face, each figure naming its face, its font-size and its probe-derived px/ch, with cross-face division BANNED (D83). A failure there is a failure; no exemption is available at those widths and none will be sought.

RULE, part 2 — WHERE IT DOES NOT APPLY, AND WHAT REPLACES IT. At `narrow` and `phone`, in the user-opened state ONLY, the bar does not apply, because no reading column is on screen to measure. This is NOT the metric being made unmeasurable: the harm this work measured was OCCLUSION of a column the reader was still trying to read, and removing the column removes the reading, not merely the measurement. The exemption is EARNED by three replacement criteria, all of which must pass or the exemption is void and Tier 3 reverts to a defect:

(a) ROUND-TRIP FIDELITY. default -> user-opened -> dismissed returns the reading column BIT-IDENTICAL to its pre-open value, at every width and every forced face, measured by the instrument in one run rather than compared across runs. A destination the reader cannot get back from is worse than an overlay.

(b) THE EXIT IS CHEAP AND PLURAL. Escape, an explicit close control, and a tap outside all dismiss; focus is trapped while summoned and restored to the invoking control on dismiss; `aria-modal` and `aria-expanded` tell the truth in every state. This is `spd-b12-inspector-overlay-dismiss`'s four criteria, and it is the SPINE of any mode claim — a mode you cannot leave is a trap, and the current one cannot be left. Note the structural constraint the survey must resolve: today's scrim is a `::after` pseudo-element with `pointer-events: none`, so it cannot carry a dismiss handler and a real element or a window-level key handler is required.

(c) THE MODE DECLARES ITSELF. No reading text is left half-legible under a scrim in any state at any width — `scrim_covers_content_fully` must be false, or the scrim absent, in every row of the successor's table. If the shipped shape still dims prose anywhere, the exemption does not apply and the cell counts as a failure.

RULE, part 3 — WHAT MAY NOT MOVE. Viewport 640 stays a named, owned shortfall (D100 as superseded by D106: 50.7ch resolved Iowan, 45.9ch forced Georgia — the '~0.2ch / ~5.4ch' figures may never be quoted, they were the user-opened state read as the default one). Viewport 500 / phone stays never-ch-gated. D107's seven desktop widths are FIXED and may not be renegotiated by any slice that consults the table.
The direction debate — the rivals, and why the winner won

RIVAL 1 — MODE BY DECREE. Change no geometry. Rule the user-opened state an exempt mode, write the rule into the charter before looking, fix only the dismissal grammar, ship. It is the cheapest candidate, it is explicitly sanctioned by D127, and it would close this work in one small wave. REFUSED. It accepts the half-state as permanent: the scrim still dims the entire content box at 55% black and the reader still watches 22.00ch of prose go grey on a single click at 1024. A mode-exemption that leaves the document visible-but-illegible under the panel is not a mode — it is exactly the INDETERMINACY the wish names as the defect, and declaring it legal does not resolve it. Worse, it forecloses Tier 2 permanently: it writes an exemption over the one width the desk could actually have paid for, and a later wave inheriting that exemption would have no reason to re-check the arithmetic.

RIVAL 2 — THE NARROW SHEET. Shrink the inspector below 300px until an in-flow dock fits at 1024. REFUSED on D126's own terms AND on content. The ceiling with the panel frozen is 90px resolved Iowan and 32.4px forced Georgia; nothing that answers to 'metadata panel' fits. And the panel is ALREADY too narrow for its contents at 300px — the overlay block in `root.html.heex` ships `.bp-doc-field { flex-wrap: wrap; }` inside it, an authored admission that the label/value rows collide, and the Relations section holds outbound references plus three groups of inbound backlinks that grow without bound. Narrowing an already-cramped panel to buy fractions of a ch, per face, is the threshold-gerrymandering D83 and D103 forbid by name.

RIVAL 3 — DRILL EVERYWHERE. Make the inspector a summoned destination at every non-`wide` width, 1024 included. This is the strongest rival and it very nearly won: one rule instead of two, one shape to build and test, no new dimension on `display_state`, no collision with the epic's 40-cell literal pin, and it satisfies the pre-registered rule cleanly. It lost on a single point: at 1024 it GIVES AWAY a MEET the desk can afford. Throwing the reader out of their document to check a slug, at a width where the arithmetic says the panel and the prose fit side by side with 60.00ch to spare, is precisely the desk failing to reason about the space it has — the charge this whole epic was filed on. Rival 3 is retained as the NAMED FALLBACK, not discarded (see the absorption below).

WHY THE LADDER WON. It is the only candidate derived from the parent epic's OWN declared priority order rather than from a preference. It converts the sharpest measured cell in the ledger into a predicted pass by arithmetic on measured inputs rather than by changing a rule or moving a threshold. And it makes the pre-registered exemption HONEST in a way no rival can: the bar is suspended only at widths where a run can demonstrate the desk had nothing left to sell — which D113 already demonstrated for 900 and below, and which the charter never even asked at 1024.
The sharpest attack on the winner

THE ATTACK. Tier 2 is bought by giving `display_state` a new input, and `display_state/4`'s 40-cell exhaustive table of hardcoded literals is, by D94's own words, 'the epic's one genuinely non-vacuous wide lock' — the only assertion in the repo that catches a regression of `collapse?/3`, proven by fault injection when its neighbouring 'bit-identical' test stayed green and was later retired by conversion. And D94's re-authored criterion 2 names 'the wide/STANDARD `display_state/4` table is unchanged, pinned by literal constants' as clause (a). Viewport 1024 is `standard`. So this wave's headline collides head-on with the lock the epic wrote to protect itself, at exactly the width it protects.

THE SECOND EDGE OF THE SAME ATTACK. The Tier 2 win is bought by making a user-visible document list DISAPPEAR on a metadata click. If that reads as the desk losing the reader's place, then a 22ch gain has been purchased with a navigation regression that no ch figure in any table will ever show — and this work has been overturned before by exactly that shape of blindness (D96: the secondary pane was dead for five waves behind green tests, because every covering test drove the socket and none drove the DOM).

HOW THE WAVE ABSORBS IT. (1) The new dimension lands as a NEW ARITY — an inspector-aware `display_state/5` delegating to an UNTOUCHED `/4` — so the 40-cell literal table stays byte-identical and D94(a) is satisfied by construction rather than by argument, and the new dimension earns its OWN exhaustive literal table, extending the lock instead of widening it. Any shape that requires editing a pinned literal is refused at Decide. (2) The disappearing-list risk becomes a first-class acceptance criterion rather than a hope: round-trip fidelity must restore the PANES and the reading column, the 44px strip must stay on screen and clickable in the yielded state, and the proof must drive a real browser rather than a socket. (3) Both edges are survey assignments below, and if the survey shows `display_state` cannot take a fifth input without disturbing the pin, the wave falls back to Rival 3 at 1024 — the two shapes share the dismissal grammar, the destination surface, the metric rule and all of the instrument work, so the fallback costs this wave ONE SLICE, never its direction. A direction whose fallback is a rival it already argued is a direction that can survive being wrong.
Standing law this wave inherits, each bought with a real failure

MEASUREMENT. Every ch figure names its face, its font-size and its probe-derived px/ch; cross-face division is BANNED (D83). `viewport 640` and `content 640` never appear bare. The user-opened verdict is quoted from `visible_meets_55ch`, never `content_meets_55ch` (D139). The 13/3 overlay-caused vs inherited decomposition is quoted decomposed. D124 and D125 are always quoted TOGETHER, as are D119 and D133. The struck figures — 420px, ~42ch, '~0.2ch / ~5.4ch', '9 of 9 default cells MEET' — may not be quoted.

THE INSTRUMENT. It has NO gate authority by design: it needs deployed guerrilla, an admin token and an authenticated Chromium run, and a flaky gate everyone learns to ignore is worse than an honest script. Observed full-sweep runtimes are 29.8s / 30.9s / 32.8s / 59.7s — the '~10 minutes' comment was off by ~20x and was a live false-blocker (D115). A run that writes ZERO BYTES is an INSTRUMENT FAILURE reported as such, never a desk fact (D130, D138). Determinism is ~80%, not 100%: the honest sentence is '4 of 5 completed runs reproduce the committed table at tolerance zero; the fifth diverged in one row outside the ruling set and the instrument caught it itself' — never '0 of 54' (D138). Bracket every sweep with a pre- AND post-run provenance read over ssh and discard on mismatch. Prove the non-vacuity guard applies in >0 rows before quoting any cell — `applies: 0` is vacuous, not a pass (D122). Register the prediction BEFORE the run so it can fail (D138).

SURFACES AND GATES. Stay in `barkpark_web`. `cloud/` belongs to the GUI-remake epic; `api/tenancy`, `internal/cli` and `scripts/` beyond this work's own instrument belong to PDS. `root.html.heex` is SINGLE-OWNER PER ROUND (D16) — two slices touching it never dispatch in the same round, and pre-provisioning CSS against an element no slice yet renders is refused (D67). Both colour gates plus `paper-editor-mirror-check` guard any `root.html.heex` touch, and the Part E ratchet fails on SHRINK too. A branch predating a token change reds `design/check.mjs` with a stale generated app.css layer — rebase, then `node design/emit.mjs --write`, and verify `node design/check.mjs` exits 0 locally before pushing. Hand-written CSS must NEVER sit inside the BEGIN GENERATED block: `emit --write` deletes it silently while the design gate goes GREEN on the deletion. `.ex`/`.exs`/`.heex` branches WAIT for the Elixir Test gate.

LEDGER. `lifecycle_status: blocked` FAILS OPEN and is DESTRUCTIVE fail-open — claiming a blocked task flips it to `in_progress` and releasing lands on `open` — so it is never a fence (D98). File ownership is enforced by the round/`after` graph and `files:` labels. Every reference is by FULL SLUG (D116, D133): `bp task get spd-b28` 404s, and worse, `bp task get spd-b35` RESOLVES SILENTLY to the wrong task. New slugs carry NO counter and NO shared wave prefix — a wave prefix is a counter wearing a different hat, and D119 reproduced under observation FOUR times, most recently inside the wave that transcribed it (D144). Line numbers are banned from briefs; navigate by marker.
